channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The Israeli elections.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, the death of the judge hearing Nicolás Maduro’s case.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Israel’s elections. On Tuesday, Israel held its first elections since Hamas’s October 7 attacks in 2023. With approximately 96% of ballots counted, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won more seats than any other party in Israel’s Knesset but will fall short of the 61 seats needed for a majority. The results set the stage for what is expected to be weeks of negotiations over a new governing coalition and Netanyahu’s future. 

Back up: Elections for the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, are held every four years. As with other parliamentary systems, individual representatives do not run for office directly; instead, national parties are assigned seats proportional to the share of the vote they receive. No Israeli party has ever won an outright majority, so party leaders must agree to a coalition government and choose a prime minister. The sides have roughly 100 days to form a government. If that process fails, Israel must hold another election within 90 days of the deadlock. 

Netanyahu’s current coalition includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish leaders who have been outspoken advocates for Israeli military operations in Gaza and across the Middle East after October 7. The prime minister’s main competitor is former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and his center-right Yashar party. Two parties predominantly representing Arab Israelis made significant electoral gains and may now attempt to join a governing coalition. 

The election’s key issues included policy toward Palestinians and Iran, exemptions from mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, and judicial reform. It was also viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership pre- and post-October 7, as well as his handling of Israel’s multi-front regional conflicts.

Currently, pro-Netanyahu parties are projected to win 53 seats, while opposition parties are expected to win 48. Roughly 78% of eligible voters participated, the highest share since 1999. Arab Israeli voters, in particular, turned out at above-average rates, and the Arab-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List are projected to win 19 combined seats in the Knesset. On Wednesday, Eisenkot said the high turnout should push party leaders to reach a governing agreement, saying, “It would be a mistake to hold another election.”

Also on Wednesday, Netanyahu claimed that Arab parties had “stolen” the election and called for investigations into “election theft in many Arab polling stations.” Israel’s Central Elections Committee said it is reviewing all election-fraud allegations. 

Today, we’ll share views from the left, right, and Israeli writers on the elections. Then, Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left scrutinize Netanyahu’s legacy.
  • Others suggest the outcome of the elections will define the future of Israel’s democratic system.

In The New York Times, Ezra Klein said “Netanyahu won the Middle East and lost the world.”

“Most Israeli Jews now see the world the way Netanyahu has long seen it. That is Netanyahu’s great victory. But it is matched by his great loss: Much of the world now sees Israel the way Gazans see it,” Klein wrote. “More limited counterterrorism approaches would have allowed Israel to hunt Hamas’s leaders without squandering the sympathy and horror the world then felt on Israel’s behalf. Restraint would have kept the focus on Hamas’s attack. 

“But Netanyahu wanted to risk more to achieve more. He flattened Gaza in search of a nebulous ‘total victory’ over Hamas — a goal prioritized over the lives not just of Gazans but of the Israeli hostages,” Klein said. “For all the damage Israel has meted out against its enemies, the Iranian regime stands. Hezbollah stands. Hamas stands. And America’s special relationship with Israel is drawing to its end.”

In Bloomberg, Marc Champion wrote about a “test [on] Israel’s democracy.”

“Two things can be said about Israel’s election on Tuesday, even though it may be days or weeks before it becomes clear who will next lead the country,” Champion said. “The first is that, as an exercise in participatory democracy, this vote was immense. An unprecedented 77% of eligible voters cared enough to vote in what amounted to a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s responsibility for, and response to, the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023. 

“The second is that this democracy could well be extinguished depending on what happens next,” Champion wrote. “A different government could halt Netanyahu’s assault on democratic institutions, in particular the courts, as well as his administration’s incitement of Palestinians through violence, and the aggressive settlement policies that are removing options for some form of peaceful coexistence… This choice is binary. It will decide which Israeli state — the secular-democratic whole or the Jewish, majoritarian one — is to be the actual Israel.”

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right say the results show Netanyahu remains a political force.
  • Others call for slow reform in the next Israeli government.

The New York Post editorial board said “Israelis have delivered their verdict.”

“Projections early on election night showed Netanyahu’s coalition with fewer seats than the ‘ditch Bibi’ alliance,” the board wrote. “Obama-era officials and armchair ‘experts’ jumped to declare that Israelis had delivered a ‘rebuke’ of Netanyahu and his war strategy. Within hours, the results were reversed: Israelis had rallied behind their prime minister; the opposition… appears to have depended too heavily on the hopes of Netanyahu-haters in the media and abroad.”

“Netanyahu should take one result to heart: The Arab parties did extraordinarily well. That refutes claims of ‘apartheid,’ but it also sends a message that hateful rhetoric from far-right Jewish politicians, and vigilante actions by extremist settlers, must end,” the board said. “In the end, Netanyahu prevailed because voters respect strength. He defeated Hamas and Hezbollah, brought back the hostages, and put Israel back on a path of economic growth. Regardless of who governs in the end, the Israeli people back Netanyahu’s tough approach to Iran.”

In the Washington Examiner, Eric Wargotz argued against “tearing [the Israeli government] down right now.”

“Almost everyone seems to agree that it is time for a change in [Israel’s] leadership. Critics are loudly calling for a new government to heal the country’s social fractures, mend broken trust, and move past recent trauma,” Wargotz wrote. “That frustration makes sense. However… forcing a sudden political shake-up during a massive, multifront war is dangerous. In a true crisis, national survival and critical U.S. strategic interests both depend on stability. 

“We must keep the current command structure intact while aggressively fixing mistakes from within… If the current government drops, it will likely be replaced by an unstable mix of opposition parties,” Wargotz said. “Spending months arguing over how to build a new coalition creates a dangerous power vacuum. During that gap, major military choices, joint intelligence work, and delicate hostage talks get stuck in political limbo. This paralysis directly undermines U.S. operational planning in the region, and Israel’s enemies will instantly exploit the hesitation.”

What Israeli writers are saying.
  • Some Israeli writers say opposition parties should reject Netanyahu.
  • Others call for a coalition government between Eisenkot and Netanyahu.

In the Middle East Eye, Meron Rapoport called the election a “wake-up call.”

“The Palestinian citizens of Israel have taught the liberal secular Zionist camp a lesson. These opposition parties were under the illusion that they could win a majority by being nationalistic, opposing the ultra-Orthodox community and associating themselves with the military. Now it is very clear that they cannot win an election without the Arabs,” Rapoport wrote. “This may open an understanding among the Jewish secular liberal camp.”

“It has two choices: live forever under Netanyahu or someone of his ilk or come to an understanding with the Arab parties and voters,” Rapoport said. “It is too early to say what will happen. The success of the Palestinian parties could prompt the right wing to do everything in its power to make sure Arab voters cannot impact elections like these ever again… Or, the liberal secular camp can turn away from its racist heritage.”

In The Jerusalem Post, Shir Perets said “it’s time to set ego aside.”

“There are some ideals we cannot stray from in a post-October 7 world, and the next Knesset cannot set itself up to be held hostage by one faction,” Perets wrote. “The solution is simple: Eisenkot and Netanyahu must set their differences aside to form a true unity government… Such an arrangement would require significant compromises from both leaders, who have spent the campaign presenting competing visions for Israel's future. 

“[Their] differences cannot simply be dismissed as personal animosity or political ego. They concern fundamental questions about accountability, democratic institutions, national security, and the direction of the state,” Perets said. “The coming negotiations will test not only the two leaders’ willingness to compromise, but also whether their respective parties and potential coalition partners are prepared to accept such an arrangement… We voted for peace and unity. It's up to them to deliver it.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • This election’s outcome challenges the way many Westerners, including me, see Israeli politics.
  • The electorate has evolved throughout Israel’s conflicts, and many voters clearly want a strongman leader.
  • I expected — even hoped for — a different result, but Netanyahu’s grip on power remains steadfast.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

In a lot of ways, it’s hard for me to understand how Benjamin Netanyahu has survived.

Many Western writers look at these Israeli elections solely through the lens of the events in Gaza — the debate over what constitutes a genocide or ethnic cleansing, Netanyahu’s culpability, and the ramifications of Israel’s response to October 7. I think Ezra Klein (under "What the left is saying”) put this Western perspective perfectly: “Most Israeli Jews now see the world the way Netanyahu has long seen it,” but “much of the world now sees Israel the way Gazans see it.”

This rings true for me.

Meanwhile, within Israel, a single perfect line to describe the electorate’s enduring support of Netanyahu is elusive. Even if Israelis have adopted the prime minister’s view of this moment — that Israel is isolated, surrounded by enemies on multiple fronts, and must respond to any threat with absolute force — how is he the leader Israelis are turning to? Netanyahu allowed the greatest security failure in modern Israeli history to happen on his watch. The attack was carried out by a group Netanyahu has been propping up for years in an effort to divide Palestinians. His excuse was, essentially, “I was sleeping.”

From a purely political standpoint, consider Netanyahu’s actions since: He has blocked investigations into the events of October 7, denied responsibility, and deflected blame onto others. In the wake of October 7, Israel has been thrust into — as Netanyahu himself has put it — a “seven-front war.” 

Safety and security, this is not. Yet Benjamin Netanyahu survives.

His popularity is particularly tough to reconcile given his chief opponent in this race. Gadi Eisenkot is not some peace-and-love lefty Israeli. He is a former general. He shares many of Netanyahu’s hawkish views, including that shows of force — even in civilian areas — can be powerful deterrents. He is now staunchly opposed to any Palestinian state and promised, if his party took power, to propose a plan to remove Hamas from power within 18 months.

At the same time, Eisenkot is also one of Netanyahu’s staunchest and most credible critics. He was the IDF’s chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, and he joined the emergency war cabinet after Hamas’s October 7 attack in 2023. Once he got an inside look at Netanyahu’s operation, he left the cabinet and called out the lack of a post-war strategy. He alleged Netanyahu was prolonging the war for his own political survival (a theory I’ve also espoused in Tangle) and criticized him for not making a deal to release the hostages sooner. He also claimed Netanyahu was “shaking like a leaf” after the attacks, frozen in fear and unsure of what to do.

Even starker is the contrast of the war’s impact on the two. Eisenkot’s children fought in the war, and one of his sons was killed (he also lost two nephews). The eulogy he gave at his son’s funeral was aired across the country and became a symbol of the pain many Israelis were experiencing in the immediate aftermath of Hamas’s attack.

Imagining that this person would place behind Netanyahu, whose eldest son is a notorious internet troll and podcast host who spends most of his time in Miami, doesn’t comport with my basic understanding of electoral politics. Which of these people is going to better connect with the Israeli public? Which of these people is a real security leader?

According to the Israeli electorate, it’s Benjamin Netanyahu. 

Like any political phenomenon, Netanyahu’s survival can’t be attributed to one thing. Some have pointed to the fact Eisenkot is a Mizrahi Jew, of Moroccan descent, and would have been the first non-Ashkenazi Jew to become prime minister. I’m sure that impacted the way he connected with voters, and Netanyahu’s media allies have made it a story.

Others point to the ultra-Orthodox wing of Netanyahu’s coalition trying to avoid military enlistment. Netanyahu has said it’s an issue to resolve post-coalition building; Eisenkot has made clear he wants them to serve like everyone else.  

Most likely, though, is that I am just disconnected from the mood on the ground in Israel, which is in favor of a “no-compromise” war. I’ve written a lot about struggling with my identity as a Zionist Jew in the post-October 7 world — how radicalized the right wing of Israel’s politics has become, and how the collective punishment of Gazans in response to the October 7 attacks (and the support for that response) has made me feel distant from people whom I used to align myself with. I haven’t set foot in Israel since I lived there in 2013, but it’s clear to me the mindset of Israelis has undergone a radical change. I get it; my mindset as an American Jew, with more awareness of the threats around me, has changed, too.

With that obstinate mood in Israel, Eisenkot’s relative level-headedness might be a weakness. One of the things Eisenkot is most famous for is his insistence, in 2016, on investigating an Israeli sergeant who shot and killed a wounded Palestinian attacker in Hebron. Other politicians wanted to shut the investigation down, but Eisenkot insisted a trial and investigation were necessary for the integrity of the IDF. He’s also opposed illegal settlements in the West Bank, calling out “Jewish terrorism,” and has said there must be a state investigation into how October 7 happened. 

To me, all of this indicates a man with a moral compass who cares about the integrity of the Israeli government and has the integrity to be a leader. But to many Israelis, it probably indicates softness — a pliability — that isn’t fit for this moment. Eisenkot has portrayed the image of a warrior and unifier, while Netanyahu has portrayed a no-mercy belligerent ready to take on the world. He can certainly argue his merciless attitude has worked: Israel just had its first 12-month span this century without a single rocket being fired from Gaza. It enlisted the U.S. in its war with Iran. It has devastated Hamas and beaten back Hezbollah in Lebanon. Netanyahu is running on these positive outcomes he achieved through maximum force. And a plurality of Israelis just showed us which image is connecting with them more in this moment.

Of course, this wasn’t a two-man race. The Arab-Israeli bloc turned out in historic fashion, which Netanyahu has responded to with the Trumpian play of alleging fraud (the turnout is historically high, but I suspect that’s due to the rampant anti-Arab sentiment being promulgated by Netanyahu’s coalition, not fraud). Aside from reminding the West that Israel is a messy, pluralistic state with many ethnicities and faiths participating in the democratic process, the Arab-Israeli turnout could force some uncomfortable coalition building and compromise in the coming weeks. The opposition bloc and Arab parties easily outnumber Netanyahu, yet Eisenkot would never partner with them wholesale. So how many Arab parties is he willing to partner with? And can he maintain his support through those negotiations? After everything that’s been said, would he consider a unity government with Netanyahu as an alternative?

Predicting how these coalitions will form is genuinely beyond my understanding of Israeli politics (or anyone’s, frankly). But I do understand that today, in one of the highest turnout elections in Israeli history, voters had a choice to end Netanyahu’s multi-decade grip over their country’s politics. After everything we’ve seen, I hoped they might decisively choose it — they didn’t, and the future now depends on a closed-door coalition arithmetic that nobody can predict.

Take the survey: What do you think of the election result? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

Alvin K. Hellerstein, a senior judge of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, passed away on Wednesday at 92 years old. President Bill Clinton appointed Hellerstein; the judge served on the bench from October 1998 until his death and oversaw a series of cases in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks. More recently, Judge Hellerstein presided over the case of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro following the leader’s capture and extradition to New York City. Maduro’s case was reassigned on Wednesday, at random, to Judge Analisa Torres of the Southern District of New York. The New York Times has the story.

item.title: The Maine Senate election.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, the latest on President Trump’s ‘anti-weaponization’ fund.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Maine Senate race. In a Senate race that could determine the majority in the upper chamber, Democrat Troy Jackson holds a narrow polling lead over Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win a Senate majority, and Collins is the only incumbent Republican senator running for reelection this year in a state that Kamala Harris (D) won in 2024. The Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato’s Crystal Ball all rate the race a toss-up, but Jackson holds a 1.2-point lead over Collins in the most recent RealClearPolitics polling average. As of Wednesday morning, 220,000 Mainers have cast early votes in the election, with registered Democrats outnumbering Republicans nearly 5:2. 

Back up: In July, Democratic candidate Graham Platner dropped out of the race after Jenny Racicot, a former girlfriend, accused him of raping her in 2021. Platner had won the Democratic primary in June with 72% of the vote. Delegates at a special nominating convention in Bangor chose Jackson to replace Platner on July 25. 

Jackson, 58, is a former logger who first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 before becoming a Democrat in 2004. He served in the Maine Legislature for nearly two decades, spending six years as Senate president. His platform includes support for Medicare for All and ending U.S. military support for Israel, and he has pledged to reject corporate PAC money. Republicans have criticized Jackson’s progressive views and questioned his temperament, pointing to an incident in 1988 when he punched a man, reports of outbursts against his state Senate colleagues, and a recent debate moment in which he told Collins to “shut up.”

Collins, 73, is seeking a sixth term as senator. She has campaigned on her bipartisan credentials, seniority on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and opposition to President Donald Trump’s signature tax and spending law. However, critics have scrutinized Collins for not casting votes that meaningfully opposed the president. Also, in September, ProPublica reported that the FBI had planned to investigate her ties to a defense contractor whose former CEO went to prison over illegal donations to her campaign. Collins called the report false. 

Maine is this cycle’s most expensive Senate race per capita, with roughly $200 million in ad spending. Republicans have spent close to $114 million, while Democrats have spent approximately $81 million. Outside groups account for 79% of all spending in the race.

Today, we’ll go over what the left and right are saying about the Maine Senate election. Then, Senior Editor Will Kaback gives his take.

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right say the Maine race is a fork in the road for the GOP.
  • Many criticize Troy Jackson, particularly for his performance in the recent debate.
  • Others question whether Collins has a strong enough record on affordability issues.

In Fox News, David Marcus argued the race will determine “the future of the GOP.”

“If Troy Jackson does manage to topple Collins, the message to Republicans in Maine and New England will be that centrism doesn’t work, that they need bare knuckle brawlers more like Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, than bipartisan peacemakers like Collins,” Marcus wrote. “[Some Republicans] see moderate Republicans as more of an obstacle than an asset. But most in the GOP concede that holding the Senate for Trump’s final two years in office outweighs the broader ideological intraparty fights.”

“Win, lose, or draw for Collins, in the future it will be younger Republican politicians… who will have to define what a Republican is in Maine, New England, and to some degree in America as a whole,” Marcus said. “If Maine Republicans can save Susan Collins once again, it will show that the GOP really can, at least in part, and unlike Democrats, embrace moderate and centrist positions — a point that could play heavily in their favor as both parties try to define themselves for the post-Trump age.”

In PJ Media, Matt Margolis said “Troy Jackson choke[d] in debate.”

“Collins crushed Jackson by exposing his thin legislative record, while he showed a lack of polish,” Margolis wrote. “She saved her one prepared question for the résumé he’s running on. ‘In your more than 20 years in the legislature, more than one third of your bills were unanimously rejected in committee… If you can’t find one person in your own party to vote for your bills when you were the Senate president in Maine, how do you think you’re going to get things done in a closely divided Senate as the most junior senator?’ she asked.”

“Collins spent the rest of the evening reminding voters what seniority buys them,” Margolis said. “Jackson is not an inspiring candidate, and he has put his foot in his mouth more than once. He ducked the question when asked whether he is a socialist, and he is out of step on voter ID… Democrats likely need to flip Maine to have any chance of taking the Senate, and polls show the race basically tied. But here’s the problem for them: past polling in Collins’ races often had Democrats up several points before she won handily. A tie suggests Jackson is in trouble.”

In USA Today, Nicole Russell suggested “Collins may have met her match in Maine.”

“Collins has trailed Jackson for weeks… She’s been through this before. In 2020, polls showed Collins trailing Democrat Sara Gideon, but she ended up winning by nearly 9 points,” Russell wrote. “Maine women could decide the race. In 2020, women made up nearly 60% of the electorate, according to NPR. They voted for Joe Biden for president by 23 points, but they also backed Sen. Collins, by 3. Jackson leads among women this time, though narrowly.”

“Abortion is an obvious point of contention, and Collins walks a tightrope on it. She supports abortion rights, but her 2018 Senate vote was crucial to Brett Kavanaugh’s confirmation to the Supreme Court,” Russell said. “But like the rest of the country right now, Maine voters, women included, seem more worried about affordability than abortion… On that issue, Collins’ ties to Trump could keep Jackson — who purports to be a champion of the working class, albeit while supporting contradictory policies — in a dead heat through Election Day.”

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left say Collins is a moderate in name only.
  • Others criticize her record on labor issues.  
  • Still others express uncertainty about Jackson’s strength as a candidate. 

In The New Republic, Jason Linkins wrote “make Susan Collins pay for her big abortion lie.”

“Somehow or another, [Collins] has managed to carve out an identity for herself as a moderate Republican, despite being a Trumpist par excellence. She’s voted with Trump 92 percent of the time,” Linkins said. “But if there is one arena in which Collins’s mendacity shines, it’s in her unearned pro-choice pretensions… Collins was asked to account for her pivotal confirmation vote for Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, whose presence on the high court all but ensured the gutting of Roe: ‘I’m very disappointed in his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade,’ Collins attested. ‘There was no way for me to anticipate that.’

“It’s pretty weird that this one Maine senator was unable to ‘anticipate’ something that the right has been working toward for the past half-century, building out an entire right-wing legal movement and funneling anti-abortion judges through the pipeline of the federal judiciary,” Linkins wrote. “How much more clarity does Susan Collins need? Hopefully, in a few short weeks, we won’t need to keep asking her.”

In Jacobin, Branko Marcetic said Collins’s record is “making injured workers’ lives harder.”

“Susan Collins has been the senator from Maine for twenty-nine years,” Marcetic wrote. “One of the most impactful measures on Maine workers that she took happened well before she first went to Washington. In an episode that’s little remembered today, in the late 1980s and early ’90s, Collins led the way on a set of reforms to Maine’s workers’ compensation system that saw the state government shut down for the first time in its history and led to major cuts to injured workers’ benefits.” 

“Collins has carved out a reputation as a moderate in the Senate,” Marcetic said. “But as her early role in cutting benefits for injured Maine workers recalls, Collins has also had a long history as an ideologically driven servant of the business sector… If Collins survives another reelection campaign this November, it will be yet another Harry Houdini–like political escape for a politician adept at putting a moderate face on a record that has been devastating for US workers.”

In The Atlantic, Tyler Austin Harper described “the contradictions of Troy Jackson.”

“Jackson seems to be attempting to pair a left-leaning, economically populist package with ‘woke’ cultural ideals, which working-class voters tend to reject,” Harper wrote. “On economic issues, Jackson is in sync with the working-class and rural voters he says he is championing. Sixty-three percent of Americans without a college degree and 76 percent of those who make less than $50,000 a year say that the government should be responsible for ensuring health-care coverage, for example. 

“On cultural matters, however, Jackson is out of step with many of those he claims to be giving a voice to. Most Americans without a college degree say that protecting gun rights is more important than gun control… These Americans are also more likely than college graduates to express negative views about illegal immigration,” Harper said. “If socialists and populists… are so wedded to progressivism that they do not compromise with the working class, the question is not simply whether such a left can win. The question is whether it truly remains left at all.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • While Maine’s Senate race is a true toss-up, I’d give Sen. Collins the edge.
  • Collins’s influential position in the Senate could be the deciding factor.
  • Both candidates have their own challenges, but I think Jackson has more to overcome.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Maine is a state of 1.4 million people whose most populous city has less than 70,000 residents and whose identity, like its compatriots in nearby Vermont and New Hampshire, is defined by a fierce independent streak. It’s a land of blueberries and potatoes, mountains and thru-hikers, loggers and lobstermen, forests and ocean. It’s my birthplace, too — and where I spent formative seasons in the Midcoast and North Woods regions. 

When you know and love a place like I do Maine, it’s odd to hear it discussed in a political context so divorced from your experience. But for the past year, beginning with the first of the Graham Platner controversies, the state has been at the center of contentious, high-stakes national stories, all of which are now coming to a head. 

The winner of Troy Jackson vs. Susan Collins could determine control of the Senate and, by extension, the course of the country over the next two years. All of this comes on the heels of Platner, the original Democratic nominee, dropping out after a sexual assault allegation and Jackson taking his place in a hastily organized nominating convention. Collins, for her part, is battling for her political life after nearly 30 years in the Senate. 

I think the polls showing the race as neck and neck are accurate, but I would give Collins the edge. I think of the Maine senator the same way Isaac thinks of Republicans in Texas: I expect she’ll win until she doesn’t. 

Still, Collins faces significant headwinds. This is her first election since the Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade, and many pro-choice Mainers view her as at least partially responsible for that outcome because she voted to confirm Justices Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh. She also voted to confirm some of the second Trump administration’s most controversial cabinet members, including Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Tulsi Gabbard, and Kristi Noem. And more recently, she’s been linked to an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving a top donor (she denies any wrongdoing and hasn’t been charged). 

The electoral salience of these stories may vary, but her biggest problem might just be the national environment. President Trump’s approval rating has reached new lows, and in tight races across the country, Democrats are tying their opponents to the president’s record, while Republicans are trying to distance themselves from it. That dynamic applies in Maine, too: Jackson’s ads stress Collins’s voting alignment with Trump, while Collins positions herself as “America’s most bipartisan senator.” A defining question of this race is which message will be more persuasive. 

And what does it mean to be “bipartisan and independent” in 2026? In many ways, it looks like Collins. GovTrack puts her almost squarely at the center of its Ideology–Leadership chart and reported that she joined bipartisan bills most frequently relative to the full Senate. A recent Bangor Daily News analysis found that, in her Senate career, Collins has cast 56 deciding votes resulting in the preferred Democratic outcome, the most votes by any senator against their own party from 1997–2026. In the 119th Congress, she’s broken from Republicans in 28.9% of votes. Along with Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), Collins has “walked the walk” most often on bucking her party. 

At the same time, those numbers need context. For one, while 56 “decisive” votes with Democrats sound like a lot, they came over a roughly three-decade career — about two per year on average. In the second Trump administration, she’s voted with Democrats just four times on decisive votes and cast 19 deciding votes to confirm Trump nominees. Furthermore, not all votes are equally meaningful; for instance, she voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but only after casting an important procedural vote that helped it advance through the Senate. Breaking with the GOP on relatively minor matters (or when her vote won’t affect the outcome) helps burnish her independent image, but on the most consequential decisions — Supreme Court justices, cabinet nominees, tax cuts — she usually sticks with her party. Collins has the numbers to back up her claim to bipartisanship, but I doubt that will mean much to voters who only remember her most impactful votes. 

With all this being said, I give Collins the edge in this race because I think she has an advantage that’s rarely discussed in national coverage: her influence in Congress. Collins is the current chair and longtime member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, a position she’s used to secure huge federal investments in Maine’s roads, bridges, ports, airports, water systems and broadband networks, as well as funding for rural hospitals, biomedical research, and health care workforce development. 

Having her in the Senate — especially when Republicans are in the majority — means having a powerful advocate capable of helping the state punch above its weight. To me, this value proposition explains Collins’s staying power more than anything else, and it makes her formidable regardless of the national environment. For all the focus on how Trump, Platner, the economy and cultural issues have shaped the race, it could come down to fundamental self-interest and which candidate is best equipped to do the work of representation. 

Even though I see Collins as the favorite, Jackson still has a very realistic path to victory. On paper, he offers many of Graham Platner’s positive traits without the controversy. As a logger and lifelong resident of the tiny town of Allagash, Maine, his working-class roots run deep. He’s a progressive whose campaign is focused on affordability, Medicare for All, abortion access, and strengthening unions. And he’s adopted much of Platner’s stick-it-to-the-man messaging.

And yet, in crucial ways, he’s missing Platner’s strengths. For all the former candidate’s flaws, Platner was a genuine force in the primary — friends in Maine of varying political stripes frequently told me about how Platner felt energizing and distinct. Even after he dropped out, I saw “Platner for Senate” signs lining the road in solidly conservative Piscataquis County this summer. He packed rallies, won support from high-profile elected Democrats, and trounced the sitting governor in the primary. Jackson isn’t that person; he’s an acceptable substitute in an unusual situation but not someone who could have won the nomination on his own. As Tyler Austin Harper (under “What the left is saying”) noted, Jackson’s campaign has tried to raise his national profile, but it hasn’t figured out how to package his progressive beliefs with the moderate, man-of-the-people image required to win in a competitive state like Maine. Their efforts often come off as cringey and inauthentic. 

The question for Jackson, then, is whether he can do enough to capitalize on the favorable national environment and voters’ desire for a change after three decades with Collins. The incumbent senator has built a career on surviving challenging circumstances. If any Republican is positioned to pull off a battleground win on a night that could otherwise go well for Democrats, it’s Susan Collins.

Take the survey: Who do you think will win? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The $8 billion farmer relief package.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Wood
item.description: Plus, looking back on the Cuban Missile Crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The farm aid package. On Monday, October 19, President Donald Trump announced the Harvest Fuel Relief Program (HFR), an $8 billion program to support farmers during a spike in diesel costs. The Department of Agriculture (USDA) will disburse the funds as one-time payments based on a formula that projects farmers’ needed aid, with the first payments potentially going out by the end of the year. 

Back up: Energy prices in the U.S. have risen substantially since the war in Iran began in February, and diesel prices hit a record-high of $6.53 a gallon in September. Many farmers use diesel-powered agricultural machinery; they also face protracted financial challenges preceding the Iran war. In December 2025, the Trump administration announced a $12 billion aid program to support farmers “in response to temporary trade market disruptions and increased production costs.”

The USDA payments are authorized under the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC), a government corporation within USDA. The CCC may borrow from the Treasury and private organizations to finance its programs, and it may accrue up to $30 billion in funding at a time. The HFR aid will be determined based on farmers’ “modeled losses” during the 2026 crop year, including Economic Research Service cost of production estimates and World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates yields and prices. 

Farm subsidies vary annually, but the federal government typically provides billions of dollars in support. In 2025, the government made $27.9 billion in direct payments to farmers, up from $10.3 billion in 2024. Furthermore, annual government payments as a share of total net farm income have ranged from 7.0% to 40.5% in the 21st century. Factoring in the $8 billion in additional aid, payments to farmers in 2026 could near 2020’s record high of $56.7 billion (in 2025 dollars).

The Trump administration indicated that payments will begin after the midterm elections, but the exact timing is uncertain. “It’s ​going to be close to the end of the year, would be my guess,” USDA official ⁠Richard Fordyce said. “We’ve still got a lot of work ahead of us to be really dialed in on a specific number. We believe that the $8 billion is close.” 

Below are views from the left and right on the program, followed by Contributing Editor Isaac Wood’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • Many on the left view the aid as a weak attempt to mitigate damage done by Trump’s policies.
  • Some say the one-time payments won’t help much.
  • Others suggest Trump’s missteps could be a political opportunity for Democrats.

In The Guardian, Steven Greenhouse argued “Trump has been a disaster for rural America.”

“Since Trump won farm country handily in 2024, many rural voters in Kansas, Iowa and elsewhere have soured on him because the price of diesel fuel, a key input for farming, has soared by nearly 70%, because farm bankruptcies have surged and because Trump’s trade wars have significantly reduced agricultural exports,” Greenhouse wrote. “When he plunged the US into the Iran war and his many trade wars, he showed little concern about what those decisions might mean for rural America.”

“Little wonder that a recent KFF/AP poll found that roughly six in 10 rural voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the economy, while about half believe the economy is in worse shape than when Trump returned to office,” Greenhouse said. “[Trump’s Harvest Fuel Relief Program seems] like a desperate, last-ditch effort to rescue Kansas’s incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall.” 

In AlterNet, Nick Hilden said “basic math reveals the flaw in Trump’s billion-dollar farm bribe.”

“The math on this bailout looks worse the more you break it down,” Hilden wrote. “Based on the latest national average of diesel prices — roughly $6.32 per AAA — that $4,250 buys about 672 gallons. Diesel fuels a wide variety of farm transport and equipment, but if you take a mid-sized tractor doing basic plowing as an example — which uses around six gallons per hour (though a large tractor doing heavy work can use upwards of 16, so the lower number is being generous) — that results in 112 hours of operation, for one machine, doing modest work.

“For larger equipment doing heavy work, that $4,250 translates into around 40 hours of operation, but the war has kept diesel prices elevated for eight months, with no sign of ending anytime soon,” Hilden said. “Considering that U.S. farms use an average of three tractors each — along with plenty of other diesel-hungry machinery — it’s clear that Trump’s big bailout is just a drop in the bucket.”

In MS NOW, Ed Gresser wrote “Trump’s policies are hammering farmers.”

“The Trump administration’s tariff hikes raised costs. The president slapped import taxes as high as 50% on a range of products including hoes and plows, barbed wire, screws, wood, pesticides, irrigation equipment and harvesters. As a result, just about everything farmers do — from putting up a fence to spraying for weeds and bugs to harvesting crops — costs more,” Gresser said. “This spring came Trump’s decision to launch a war with Iran. The consequent halt to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz first spiked global fertilizer prices — up 20% from when the president was inaugurated — and then hit diesel fuel even harder.”

“The administration’s response has been a series of Band-Aids, with improvised emergency aid packages… But as rising bankruptcies show, these measures haven’t healed the wounds the administration’s policies have inflicted,” Gresser wrote. “The Republican Party’s hold on politics in rural America has shaped policy, government and law for 20 years. Trump’s decision to upend the farm economy has shaken it.”

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right suggest Trump is trying to paper over bad policy with handouts. 
  • Others say farmers’ struggles highlight the need for greater U.S. energy independence.
  • Still others question the funding mechanism that allows for these payments.

The Washington Post editorial board wrote “farmers need free markets, not free money.”

“Farmers face real hardships,” the board said. “Diesel prices per gallon have risen about 75% and trade disruptions from the Iran war have boosted fertilizer prices. Pointless trade wars and tariffs have reduced foreign markets where American farmers can sell their crops and have raised prices for equipment. Ranchers have also voiced frustration at the chilling effect immigration raids have had on the meatpacking workforce.

“Instead of rolling back those disruptive policies, the president is dangling money… Once government starts compensating industries whenever inputs become unexpectedly expensive, there is no principled stopping point,” the board wrote. “Bailouts socialize losses while leaving profits private. No one is going to ask farmers to pay this money back when crop prices rise and fuel prices fall.”

In the American Thinker, Cole Ellison argued “temporarily higher prices at the gas pump must not deter America from defeating Iran.”

“When the dollar amount [of the Iran war] rolls over on the pump, it hits truck drivers, tradesmen, farmers, and families trying to get by,” Ellison wrote. “Still, there is a difference between suffering for something worthwhile and suffering in vain… I do not want an endless war. I also do not want my children to deal with this conflict because we neglected to resolve it. Above all, I want to teach them that America does not abandon every difficult situation the moment it becomes expensive or inconvenient.”

“This crisis should serve as a wake-up call. We should not have to look at the price of diesel and realize that a hostile government can reach into the pockets of American families. We should not be so dependent on foreign supply chains that a conflict overseas threatens our ability to build, produce, and defend ourselves,” Ellison said. “America must be strong enough to confront its enemies abroad and strong enough to stand on its own at home.”

In National Review, John R. Puri said “Trump pays off farmers by decree, yet again.”

“With the new program, farmers are set to receive a record-high $55 billion in direct federal payments in 2026, including $14 billion in commodity-support programs and almost $30 billion in ad-hoc disaster relief,” Puri wrote. “Why even bother asking Congress in the first place? Under an archaic New Deal entity called the Commodity Credit Corporation, the president can borrow up to $30 billion from the Treasury to finance farm payments, and Congress is obligated by law to replenish the account’s ‘losses,’ meaning deliberate handouts, ex post facto. The result is a nearly unrestricted slush fund for agricultural bailouts and payoffs.”

“Congress should reform or abolish the slush fund and retake exclusive control of farm subsidies, of course, but it won’t. Why put your vote on spending decisions with price tags and trade-offs when the president can make those calls for you?” Puri asked. “This is no way to govern in a republic, where power is supposed to be exercised by the people’s elected representatives. Legislators have surrendered their constitutional duty to control the fisc, and Americans, in the end, will foot the bill.”

My take.
Isaac Wood
Contributing Editor
 
 
  • The aid package is clearly a short-term solution to much deeper problems. 
  • We should support farmers, but this isn’t the way to do it. 
  • There’s no easy fix to the underlying issues, but we can do better than band-aid fixes.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

A couple of things about this bailout are transparent. First, the motivation: High gas prices make farming more expensive and drive up grocery costs, so President Trump is worried about Republicans losing midterm votes from disgruntled farmers in Midwestern swing states and food-eaters everywhere. 

Diesel prices are hitting record highs, and the food we eat — or at least that I eat — requires farmers to use a lot of diesel fuel. As of 2023, diesel technology powers more than two thirds of all farming equipment and is used to transport 90% of agricultural products. Vehicles, machinery, and fuel account for over 10% of farmers’ input costs. More than likely, the food you eat tonight made it to your table because of diesel fuel — for better or for worse. And this year, that dependence comes with a high cost. 

Second, the bailout is transparently a band-aid fix, one that immediately covers the short-term cost of fuel for farmers feeling the strain of diesel prices. Band-aids do good work in this world. When it comes to bailouts, though, I’m worried that federal ag policy uses them to cover up deep gashes in America’s agriculture sector.

In this specific case, the $8 billion is meant to address high fuel costs from the Iran War, rather than fixing that problem by ending the war. Trump’s critics are correct that tariffs and the war have exacerbated a range of issues in the agricultural sector, but bailouts like this one obscure other, foundational problems too.  

Last year, the Trump administration rolled out a $12 billion farm bailout for “American Farmers Impacted by Unfair Market Disruptions,” which followed a $10 billion bailout at the end of the Biden administration. The USDA reported that between 2016 and 2024, the two presidents distributed over $232 billion in direct payments to farmers. That’s a lot of money. 

These bailouts ignore market signals and fail to address the breadth of underlying problems in agriculture. 

It’s like a little league team whose shortstop happens to be the coach’s son. Sometimes the coach’s kid is the best option, but other times they’re not. Repeated errors — missed ground balls or overthrows to first base — reveal when a player shouldn’t be in that position. But if that kid’s dad is the coach, then those signals can be conveniently ignored. 

Bailouts are like that. Something isn’t going right, but when problems arise — when farmers can’t afford their operating costs — the government ignores the signals by covering the costs of fuel.

I’ve never tried to make a living off of sorghum or wheat in a bad energy market; I’ve never plowed a field or even tended a garden. I know from friends and books that harvest season is incredibly difficult. Long days and sleepless nights. I can only imagine the relief that many farmers felt in their bones when they found out they might get some help paying for gas, and that relief is good. 

But if this type of payment is perpetuating more foundational problems, then it’s only delaying more grief into the future. 

Most other farmers’ organizations that give a “thank you” also mention the need for long-term solutions. Rob Larew, president of the National Farmers Union (NFU), said, “The need for repeated emergency aid is a clear sign that the farm safety net is failing family farmers. We need to provide long-term certainty and investment in diversifying our fuel sources with renewable options, not a cycle of ad hoc relief.” Several organizations call for de-regulating the use of E15, a fuel that contains 15% ethanol rather than the typical 10% ethanol. Of course they do; ethanol depends on corn production. But NFU is right that the need for repeated relief points to underlying problems.

As Jesse Allen from Agriculture of America put it, “[This bailout] will probably keep some operators in business who’ve overleveraged themselves past the point of no return.” To be blunt, a lot of individual farmers make decisions that lead to bad and brittle systems. Farming families know which practices are good, but they also know what the government wants them to do. Since the 1970s — when Agriculture Secretary Earl Butz was saying “get big or get out” — the federal government has been subsidizing inefficient market practices and questionable agricultural decisions. As Managing Editor Ari Weitzman wrote last year, subsidies incentivize farmers to plant and grow row crops and to squeeze as much output as possible, bringing huge yields in corn and soy. “But that oversaturates the global market to the point that soybeans now cost more to grow than they do to buy, a boon for the buyers’ market dominated by a small number of companies, requiring taxpayer subsidies to keep individual farmers afloat,” he said.  

Government payments have grown from $2.5 billion in 1949 to $27.9 billion in 2025 (adjusted to 2025 dollars), encouraging practices that increase overall yield but decrease the amount of profit made per yield. That becomes an endless cycle driving the need for more yield higher and higher and higher. Altogether, the whole system encourages agricultural practices that are bad for soil health, bad for the American diet, and bad for farmers — the cycle perpetually makes it harder to stay profitable.

It’s a big, complicated mess with no easy fix. But bailouts aren’t a fix at all. At this point, I can think of two options to address the industry’s underlying issues: One, build a long-term plan for removing subsidies in a way that doesn’t blow up the current system and leave farmers without livelihoods and people without food. Two, continue utilizing subsidies but enact reform so that the subsidies incentivize more efficient and healthier practices. But Trump isn’t doing either of these things. He isn’t adhering to any guiding principles about how market control can boost affordability, nor is he adhering to the free-market principle that says markets will balance themselves out if they’re left to their own devices. 

So what principle guided this decision? It’s simple: the band-aid principle. Trump’s public-opinion Spidey-sense is blaring “EMERGENCY,” so he pulls the nearest lever. His erratic behavior added costs to farmers’ ledgers, and he wants to fix it. The federal government has sent farmers bailouts before, so why not try it again? But almost by definition, short-term fixes can’t account for agriculture’s complex challenges.

The agricultural industry is built on a faulty foundation of subsidies, and the current process — bailout, high prices, bailout, high prices — obscures those faults and further weakens the foundation.

Staff concurrence.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
I agree with Isaac’s overall points about this issue: Trump is putting a band-aid over self-inflicted wounds. Diesel costs are spiking because of the Iran war (just as costs spiked last year because of tariff disruptions), and this band-aid won’t address those issues.
 
However, I’d say the issue here is deeper than we can even see: As Americans, we are completely disconnected from our food systems and have no sensitivity to the problems that threaten them. Even this issue won’t impact your grocery costs that much. As I discussed last December, a lot of what farmers grow doesn’t become your food — only about a quarter of all the calories we grow become human food (a lot becomes animal feed), and much of that gets exported. Nearly half of crop receipts are corn and soy, and only 10% of those foods become domestic foodstuffs. Meanwhile, diesel accounts for 3.3% of input costs across the agricultural sector, which is heavily weighted by corn and soy, while most produce (like spinach) is even less reliant.
 
Diesel will certainly impact prices because of its role in transportation, but that’s true of any good. Long story short: You’re not really going to feel increased fuel costs in your grocery prices too much, relative to baseline inflation. And you won’t feel the temporary relief farmers are getting in this $8 billion bailout, either. In fact, you’re not going to feel the issues impacting most farmers at all — because most of what our agricultural system grows isn’t your food. We grow commodities in search of a use.
 
That’s a problem. I’d actually say it’s THE problem here that has to be addressed from the ground up. So when Isaac talks about the deep gashes this bailout is addressing, I’d say that’s underselling it. Until we completely rework our agricultural system to help farmers grow food, we’re putting band-aids on a cancer patient.

Take the survey: Do you think this aid program will help farmers? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: An election challenge in Alaska.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Could a second Dan Sullivan upend the Senate race?
item.content:encoded:
President Trump was always going to cast doubt on the results of the 2026 midterms. 

For six years now, I’ve been writing about the various ways the president and his allies have questioned the integrity of our elections. And when they lose (or expect to lose) races they care about, those questions evolve into outright challenges. 

The president refused to accept the 2020 election results when he lost, and he even refused to accept the margins by which he won elections in 2016 and 2024. It’s equally likely he will not accept whatever happens to his preferred candidate in 2028, presuming he doesn’t attempt to find a legal pathway to a third term (and I don’t think he will).

So I wasn’t exactly surprised to see the Department of Justice announce its preemptive lawsuit about the results in Alaska. Nor was I surprised to see Trump say openly that he had instructed the DOJ to file the lawsuit, a confession that would have been a monthslong scandal in any other administration. And yet…

And yet. 

The situation in Alaska is quite preposterous.

Over the summer, The New York Times sent a reporter to meet “candidate” Daniel J. Sullivan, and it discovered the following: Daniel J. Sullivan has never before run for office. He has voted for the Democratic candidate in the last three presidential elections and has never voted for Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent he’s running against. He attends “No Kings” protests and is politically active against the Trump administration.

Despite that, he registered as a Republican just two days before he filed to run in the Senate race. Later, when corresponding with the Division of Elections about his candidacy, he gave his name as “Dan S. Sullivan,” despite his middle name starting with a “J” (Sen. Sullivan’s middle name just happens to start with an “S”). He chalked this up to a “typo,” even though the “J” and “S” are on opposite sides of the keyboard (if it were actually a typo, I’ll leave it to you to decide what kind of galactic coincidence it is that the typo produced an “S”).

On his campaign website, the challenging Sullivan uses a similar Alaskan flag theme as the Republican incumbent, with the same color schemes and stars. Yet, on Daniel J. Sullivan’s website, there are no policy positions outlined. 

He is not campaigning. 

He is hardly raising money. 

He doesn’t seem to be trying to win at all. 

So: Does anyone actually think this is anything but an attempt to undermine Sen. Dan S. Sullivan? I don’t see any reason to pretend. Daniel J. Sullivan hired the longtime Democratic consultant Amber Lee to help him file (again, as a Republican — and again, with the same name as the sitting Republican senator). When asked about this by The Times, he demurred, saying he didn’t want to talk about it because of ongoing litigation. He conceded that he figured his name would offer “an instant megaphone” for his campaign, though he hasn’t used that megaphone to do much campaigning, if any. The duplicitous candidate has played coy, but his intentions seem transparent. 

Now: How big of an impact will this have on the election? My guess is very, very little. This is a ranked-choice election, so Daniel J. Sullivan is likely to be eliminated after the first round (assuming no candidate gets to 50% immediately). Even in an election where only a few hundred thousand people will cast votes, I have a hard time imagining a scenario where the challenging Sullivan will make a big difference. I’m also happy to cede that only the least informed voters here will get confused, and even then they can still simply vote for both Sullivans. Kudos to Alaska’s election officials, who — recognizing they can’t remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot — have done a great job making sure everyone knows who is who:

How each candidate will appear on the ballot

None of this adds up to an election that has been compromised, or an election whose results are preemptively corrupted. The DOJ insisting an election result not be certified before the election takes place, in the event its preferred candidate loses by a certain number of votes, is ludicrous and dangerous. The annoying truth is that there may actually be some genuine Daniel J. Sullivan voters out there. Every election has protest votes (my dad is a poll worker in Pennsylvania, and he has to stay late counting ballots for Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck every year). If Republicans and Democrats can’t win a vote from disaffected Alaskans over a pretend candidate like this, that’s more a party problem than a Daniel J. Sullivan problem.

And yet.

Get more of the story...
We broke down the lawsuit with just the facts, and then we picked out the best arguments from conservative, progressive, and independent writers in today's free newsletter so you can make up your own mind. Read them here. 

I can’t focus all my ire on the Trump administration. I have plenty to spare for Daniel J. Sullivan, who is clearly trying to siphon votes from the Republican Party and upend the already sensitive ranked-choice voting election in Alaska.

To be honest, I’m exhausted by these dirty tricks and the partisans who defend them. In Texas, right-wing activists generated a totally made-up “mental health crisis” story about James Talarico and seemed to send out fliers and texts pretending to be trans organizations. All the while, they’ve run AI-generated ads of Talarico scribbling notes in a Bible and reading made-up passages. They do this instead of honestly campaigning on the issues or promoting their candidate to the electorate. Republicans and Democrats are both running fake news websites boosting their own candidates. Republicans and Democrats are both putting money into the other party’s primaries to fund candidates they think they’ll beat in a general election, rather than spending on their preferred candidates. 

It goes on and on and on like this — cheap, dirty, lame political plays from people who can’t win with an affirmative message about what they’ll do. And that’s to say nothing of the gerrymandering or robocalls or vicious and desperate personal attack ads permeating this year’s midterms. 

So, do I worry about the Trump administration preemptively challenging an election result before election day? Of course. I’m gearing up for a long, arduous, infuriating post-election series of denials and conspiracy theories that I’ll have to write about here. But also, in this specific case, I think Republicans’ frustration is warranted. In fact, I blame Daniel J. Sullivan for giving Trump a politically defensible reason for challenging the election results. Democrats would be just as mad, and probably just as litigious, if a Republican voter with the same name as their incumbent candidate got on the ballot as a Democrat with the help of a Republican operative in a competitive Senate race while not actually campaigning, running on any specific issues, or even trying to win.

For all of that, Daniel J. Sullivan — like election deniers and political tricksters trying to corrupt an otherwise functioning electoral system — deserves our scorn.

Moved by the take? Share it!
Staff concurrence.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
I’m in lockstep with Isaac on the second Sullivan — I believe he’s a sham candidate who entered the race to sabotage Sen. Sullivan. And yet… the DOJ’s lawsuit concerns me more.
 
RedState’s Ward Clark is an unabashedly pro-Trump commentator, but I thought he made the most principled point against the DOJ’s lawsuit of all the writers we surveyed today: “No matter what we suspect about Daniel J. Sullivan’s motivations… the only thing that matters here is that Daniel J. Sullivan followed all of the legal procedures and requirements to run for this office.”
 
More specifically, Republicans challenged the unaffiliated Sullivan’s candidacy, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he qualified for the ballot. In that case, what grounds does the Justice Department have to bring a preemptive suit? Cato’s Walter Olson and the Election Law Blog’s Rick Hasen both noted that the DOJ’s reading of the National Voter Registration Act assumes the federal government has the power to interfere with states’ certification of their elections (and possibly other state election processes). It’s a tortured interpretation of the law, and one that, if affirmed, would dissolve the constitutional boundary between federal and state governments in administering elections.
 
Fortunately, I don’t think the lawsuit will succeed. But even as I share Isaac’s (and Republicans’) frustration with what’s playing out in Alaska’s Senate race, I’m much more alarmed by the power the DOJ seeks to assert in its response.

item.title: The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Could a second Dan Sullivan upend the Senate race?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued Alaska and its Division of Elections director, seeking to preemptively block certification of the state’s Senate election if it is impacted by “voter confusion.” The closely contested race features two candidates named Dan Sullivan; Dan S. Sullivan is the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J. Sullivan is a challenger with no party affiliation. The lawsuit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race “with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan.” Attorneys for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola have asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit. 

Back up: Alaska uses a top-four primary system, in which the four candidates who receive the most votes (regardless of party) advance to the general election. In this year’s Senate race, former Rep. Peltola (D), Sen. Sullivan (R), Sullivan (no affiliation), and Gerald Heikes (R) advanced to the general election; Peltola and Sen. Sullivan received 49.5% and 41.4% of the primary vote, respectively. The state uses ranked-choice voting for federal and state general elections.

Daniel J. Sullivan, the unaffiliated candidate, is a retired teacher who has not previously held elected office. In May, he announced his candidacy as a Republican, which the Alaska Republican Party challenged. The state’s Division of Elections issued a preliminary finding in June that Sullivan was likely ineligible to run and would be disqualified; however, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled later that month that Sullivan must be included on the primary ballot. To resolve potential confusion over the two candidates, the Division of Elections said the senator should appear with the identifier “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” while the other Sullivan would have “No Party Affiliation.”

The unaffiliated Sullivan has rejected claims that he is running to undermine Sen. Sullivan’s campaign, saying he has long thought about running for office. He has done minimal campaigning, and public records show his campaign has raised negligible funds.

On Friday, President Donald Trump said he directed the Justice Department to file its lawsuit, claiming that Democrats had compelled the second Sullivan to run. The suit similarly argues, “The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.” The plaintiffs request that Alaska halt certification until an investigation can determine whether any votes were cast for the wrong candidate.

In their motion to dismiss the suit, Peltola and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee say the action is part of “a nationwide attack on free elections by the federal government” and “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) also questioned the Justice Department’s suit, writing on X, “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.” 

Today, you’ll read arguments from the right and left about the suit, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right say the Justice Department is responding properly to manipulative election tactics. 
  • Some suggest the suit is likely to fail. 
  • Others doubt the second Sullivan’s motives, but say he still has a right to run.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board wrote about “exposing ‘Decoy Dan’ in Alaska.”

“Democrats pulled a dirty trick by enlisting a decoy, Daniel J. Sullivan, to run against Republican Alaska Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Now they are indignant that the Trump Administration on Thursday filed a lawsuit that calls attention to their subterfuge,” the board said. “Democrats deny they are behind the ruse, but their fingerprints are all over it. Daniel J. Sullivan voted for Democrats in the prior three presidential elections and for Democratic nominee Mary Peltola when she ran for the House. There’s evidence that a Democratic consultant also helped launch his campaign.

“Polls show the Senate race within one or two percentage points. That means the election could be decided by a few thousand votes or less,” the board wrote. “Alaska’s convoluted ranked-choice voting system increases the risk of voter confusion. The lawsuit is a legal Hail Mary, but its real purpose before the election is to educate Alaska voters now beginning to pay attention about the Democratic trick. Who’s really undermining trust in elections?”

In Cato at Liberty, Walter Olson argued the suit is “abusive in its intentions.”

“[The suit] borders on frivolous because it attempts to stretch a federal statute, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), beyond recognition by snipping language from the law’s preamble and treating it as if it creates vast and open-ended new duties that the federal government can enforce on states,” Olson wrote. “That is not a natural reading of the text, nor is it one that courts have taken. If accepted, it would suddenly federalize many issues of local election administration.”

“It invites suspicions of bad faith by omitting any acknowledgment that Alaska’s printed ballot labels one of the two Sullivans distinctly as ‘incumbent,’ thus helping dispel confusion for a reasonable voter. In so doing, Alaska has addressed the hazard without walking into a different hazard (curbing voter choice by striking an otherwise qualified candidate),” Olson said. “The issue in question is one for the Alaska Supreme Court to decide under Alaska law, and the Alaska court did just that.”

In RedState, Ward Clark said the race “just got more complicated.”

“[The Justice Department] appear[s] to be judging the unknowable intentions of Daniel J. Sullivan in deciding to run for the United States Senate. That’s more or less what the Alaska Division of Elections did last summer, and that didn't work then. I doubt it will work now,” Clark wrote. “I happen to believe that Daniel J. Sullivan did precisely what this lawsuit maintains — he ran as a spoiler, to try to muddy the waters and siphon votes away from the incumbent. But the Alaska Division of Elections can’t read minds, and neither can the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.”

“There’s a matter of principle here, and the thing about principles is that they must be applied in the same way in every case,” Clark said. “In this case, no matter what we suspect about Daniel J. Sullivan’s motivations (and I'd bet money on them), the only thing that matters here is that Daniel J. Sullivan followed all of the legal procedures and requirements to run for this office. He did so.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the suit, arguing it was brought too close to the election.
  • Some say the DOJ’s legal arguments are deeply flawed.
  • Others suggest Trump is working to sow doubt about the midterm results.

In Vox, Ian Millhiser wrote “Trump is trying to overturn an election that hasn’t happened yet.” 

“Sen. Sullivan will be identified as a ‘Registered Republican’ and as the ‘Incumbent,’ so voters will be told which Dan Sullivan to vote for if they wish to reelect the one who is actually a senator,” Millhiser said. “Additionally, Alaska uses ranked-choice voting… So an Alaska voter who wants to reelect the Dan Sullivan who is actually a senator, but who is confused as to which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent, can simply rank both Dans Sullivan as their top two choices.”

“Even if Trump’s Justice Department had a persuasive argument that leaving not-Senator Sullivan on the ballot is illegal, they should still lose Alaska because they waited too long to file the case,” Millhiser wrote. “[The Supreme Court has] read this ‘Purcell principle’ quite expansively to forbid federal courts from issuing election-related decisions in the months leading up to an election… If Purcell means anything, it must mean that a federal court cannot force Alaska to kick a candidate off the ballot mere days before a federal election.”

In the Election Law Blog, Rick Hasen argued “the Major Questions Doctrine alone should doom [the suit].”

“[The] DOJ grasps at straws to find some power, any power, contained in a federal statute to give it the authority it demands: to block the certification of a U.S. Senate winner in Alaska until a court can (somehow) investigate possible voter confusion over candidate names,” Hasen said. “The federal government does not even rely upon the part of a law that gives the federal government any power. It instead relies upon some vague statements of purpose of the National Voter Registration Act about the importance of election integrity.”

“Did Congress in the preface to a law about voter registration give DOJ roving power to block state election certification — and presumably other state election processes — in the name of promoting the integrity of the electoral process?” Hasen asked. “The claims to federal power are as ludicrous as they are dangerous. Accepting them would fundamentally change how elections are conducted in America, and shift power away from the states and Congress… to the executive branch.”

In CNN, Aaron Blake said the lawsuit “should raise eyebrows.”

“[The suit signals] a very notable willingness by Trump’s DOJ to engage in highly questionable behavior to try and put its thumb on the electoral scale,” Blake wrote. “[It is] not at all clear how an investigation would ever ascertain how many votes Sen. Sullivan lost due to voter confusion. This issue has already been litigated extensively in court, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the Daniel J. Sullivan was qualified for the ballot. So this looks like an effort to inject doubt if Peltola wins.”

“And then there’s Trump outright saying he directed his DOJ to file the lawsuit, which carries obvious implications for him politically. That’s not surprising at this point… but it’s still highly problematic,” Blake said. “The 2020 election showed that lawsuits don’t need to succeed to have an impact. Trump’s many wild and false claims of mass voter fraud whipped his supporters into a frenzy… Even absent threats of a violent uprising, these kinds of legal efforts could deliver a pretext for other extraordinary action related to the election.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • All signs suggest that Daniel J. Sullivan launched his campaign to sow confusion in the election.
  • That doesn’t justify the DOJ preemptively challenging the election results.
  • However, it is another chapter in the ongoing election chicanery both parties have been undertaking for decades, and it’s exhausting.
